items.label: f02-fetch-404-resolves
items.front: A data loader wraps `await fetch(url)` and `await response.json()` in try/catch and assumes the catch handles every failure. The server returns 500 with an HTML error page. What happens?
items.back: fetch only rejects on network failures; a 500 resolves, so the code goes on to parse the error page (a confusing JSON parse error or bad data). Fix: check `response.ok` and throw with the status before parsing.

items.label: f03-or-default-drops-zero
items.front: Settings load with `volume = saved.volume || 50`. A user who muted (saved volume 0) reloads the page. What do they hear?
items.back: Volume 50: `||` falls back on any falsy value, so the legitimate 0 is discarded. Fix: `saved.volume ?? 50`, which falls back only on null or undefined.

items.label: f04-null-property-read
items.front: A receipt page renders `order.customer.email`. Guest checkouts store `customer: null`. What happens for a guest order?
items.back: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'email'), and the page crashes. Fix: guard the null (check first) or use optional chaining `order.customer?.email` with a fallback.

items.label: f01-sort-mutates-caller
items.front: A helper `cheapestFirst(prices)` returns `prices.sort()`. After calling it, the caller's original price list is reordered and shows [1, 10, 100, 9]. What went wrong?
items.back: sort() sorts in place (the caller's array is mutated) and with no comparator compares as strings. Fix: copy first and pass a comparator, `[...prices].sort((a, b) => a - b)`, or use toSorted.

items.prompt: Three click handlers are created in `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) handlers.push(() => i)`. Every handler reports 3. Why, and what is the smallest fix?

choices.text: `i++` mutates a global variable shared by every script on the page, so renaming the loop variable fixes it
Arrow functions copy `i` when they are called, not created, so `function () { return i; }` fixes it
`var` gives the function one `i` that every closure shares; declare it with `let` for a binding per iteration
The closures capture `i` by value, but `push` runs after the loop ends, so move it before the increment

choices: `i++` mutates a global variable shared by every script on the page, so renaming the loop variable fixes it
Arrow functions copy `i` when they are called, not created, so `function () { return i; }` fixes it
`var` gives the function one `i` that every closure shares; declare it with `let` for a binding per iteration
The closures capture `i` by value, but `push` runs after the loop ends, so move it before the increment

items.explanation: With var there is one i for the whole function, so all closures see its final value 3; with let each loop iteration gets its own binding, so the closures return 0, 1, 2.

items.prompt: A reviewer deletes the trailing `0` from `cart.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p.price, 0)` because the tests (all with non-empty carts) still pass. What breaks in production?

choices.text: Every total becomes a string, since the first product object becomes the accumulator
Nothing breaks: reduce defaults the accumulator to 0 when the callback adds numbers
An empty cart now totals `undefined`, which renders as a blank price but never throws
An empty cart now throws a TypeError, because reduce is left with no starting value

choices: Every total becomes a string, since the first product object becomes the accumulator
Nothing breaks: reduce defaults the accumulator to 0 when the callback adds numbers
An empty cart now totals `undefined`, which renders as a blank price but never throws
An empty cart now throws a TypeError, because reduce is left with no starting value

items.explanation: Always give reduce a starting value; without it, reduce on an empty array throws a TypeError because there is nothing to start from.

items.prompt: A search page renders the results list `if (results)` and otherwise shows "No matches". With zero matches the API returns `[]` and the page shows an empty list instead of the message. Why?

choices.text: An empty array is an object, and every object is truthy, so the `if` check passes
Arrays coerce to their first element, and `if` treats the undefined from `[]` as true
`[]` is falsy, but the check ran before the fetch resolved and saw an older value
`if` on an array variable only checks that it was declared, not what it contains

choices: An empty array is an object, and every object is truthy, so the `if` check passes
Arrays coerce to their first element, and `if` treats the undefined from `[]` as true
`[]` is falsy, but the check ran before the fetch resolved and saw an older value
`if` on an array variable only checks that it was declared, not what it contains

items.explanation: Empty arrays and empty objects are truthy; use results.length > 0 when you mean 'if there are items'.

items.prompt: `const DEFAULTS = { theme: "light" }` is shared by every page. One page does `DEFAULTS.theme = "dark"` and now all pages are dark. Why didn't `const` prevent this?

choices.text: `const` protects top-level properties except strings, which are shared by reference
`const` freezes objects only in strict mode, and that page was not in strict mode
The assignment created a new DEFAULTS that shadows the shared one in every module
`const` only stops the name from being rebound; the object itself stays fully mutable

choices: `const` protects top-level properties except strings, which are shared by reference
`const` freezes objects only in strict mode, and that page was not in strict mode
The assignment created a new DEFAULTS that shadows the shared one in every module
`const` only stops the name from being rebound; the object itself stays fully mutable

items.explanation: const means the label cannot be pointed somewhere else; it says nothing about whether the object can change (use Object.freeze or copies).

items.prompt: A refactor changes `prices.map(p => p * 1.1)` to `prices.map(p => { p * 1.1 })` to make room for a log line. The resulting array is all `undefined`. Why?

choices.text: map skips callbacks that declare a block scope, leaving the new array's slots empty
Braces turn the expression into a function body, which needs an explicit return
Braces make the arrow return an object literal, which map cannot use as a number
The multiplication runs after map finishes, because a block body runs asynchronously

choices: map skips callbacks that declare a block scope, leaving the new array's slots empty
Braces turn the expression into a function body, which needs an explicit return
Braces make the arrow return an object literal, which map cannot use as a number
The multiplication runs after map finishes, because a block body runs asynchronously

items.explanation: An arrow with a single expression after => returns it automatically; as soon as you add { }, you must write return, and a body without one returns undefined.

items.prompt: A test calls `addToCartTotal(10)` (which does `cart.total += amount`) and asserts 10. It passes alone but fails when run after another test. Why is `withItemAdded(total, amount)` easier to test?

choices.text: The first reads and changes shared state, so its result depends on earlier calls
The pure version is easier only because its second parameter lets tests pass the cart
Shared objects reset between tests automatically, so the failure is floating-point drift
The first is slower because it writes to an object, so it times out after other tests

choices: The first reads and changes shared state, so its result depends on earlier calls
The pure version is easier only because its second parameter lets tests pass the cart
Shared objects reset between tests automatically, so the failure is floating-point drift
The first is slower because it writes to an object, so it times out after other tests

items.explanation: addToCartTotal depends on and changes hidden shared state; the pure version returns the same output for the same inputs. Side effects are not bad, but keeping decision logic pure makes it easy to test and reuse; keep side effects at the edges.

items.prompt: Code calls `loadPosts()` (an async function that awaits fetch) and on the next line reads the list it fills. The list is still empty. Why?

choices.text: Async functions return undefined immediately, so a caller can never see the list filled
`await` suspends only loadPosts; the caller keeps running unless it awaits too
fetch responses are cached, so the second line read a stale, empty cached response
`await` blocks the whole program, but DOM updates are batched until the next frame

choices: Async functions return undefined immediately, so a caller can never see the list filled
`await` suspends only loadPosts; the caller keeps running unless it awaits too
fetch responses are cached, so the second line read a stale, empty cached response
`await` blocks the whole program, but DOM updates are batched until the next frame

items.explanation: await pauses only inside the current async function, not the entire program; the caller reads the list before the request finishes and must await the returned promise.

items.prompt: An API returns `{ name: null }` for anonymous users and the UI calls `greet(user.name)` with `function greet(name = "friend")`. Users see "Hi, null". Why didn't the default kick in?

choices.text: Defaults apply only to omitted arguments, so any explicit value, even undefined, skips it
Defaults treat every falsy argument as missing except null, which marks an intentional value
The default is evaluated once at definition and was overwritten by an earlier named call
A default parameter is used only when the argument is undefined; null is a real value

choices: Defaults apply only to omitted arguments, so any explicit value, even undefined, skips it
Defaults treat every falsy argument as missing except null, which marks an intentional value
The default is evaluated once at definition and was overwritten by an earlier named call
A default parameter is used only when the argument is undefined; null is a real value

items.explanation: greet(undefined) gives 'Hi, friend' but greet(null) gives 'Hi, null': null is passed through unchanged. Normalize null to undefined (or use ??) at the boundary.

items.prompt: A quantity validator does `if (Number.isNaN(Number(input))) reject()`. A user leaves the field blank and an order for 0 items goes through. Why?

choices.text: Number("") is 0, not NaN, so a blank field passes the NaN check and counts as zero
Blank inputs are submitted as null, and Number(null) is NaN only in strict mode
Number.isNaN coerces its argument first, so "" counts as a valid number
Number("") throws, the form library swallows it, and the default 0 is used

choices: Number("") is 0, not NaN, so a blank field passes the NaN check and counts as zero
Blank inputs are submitted as null, and Number(null) is NaN only in strict mode
Number.isNaN coerces its argument first, so "" counts as a valid number
Number("") throws, the form library swallows it, and the default 0 is used

items.explanation: Number("") is 0, a common source of 'empty field counted as zero' bugs; check for blank input separately.

items.prompt: An edit form starts from `draft = { ...profile }` and the user changes `draft.address.city` before pressing Cancel. Why does the saved profile show the new city anyway?

choices.text: `profile` was declared with const, and const objects forward writes made to their copies
Spread is shallow, so `address` is still the very same nested object the profile holds
Cancel re-runs the spread in reverse, merging the draft's fields back into the profile
Spread copies nested objects but keeps their getters linked, so city changes sync back

choices: `profile` was declared with const, and const objects forward writes made to their copies
Spread is shallow, so `address` is still the very same nested object the profile holds
Cancel re-runs the spread in reverse, merging the draft's fields back into the profile
Spread copies nested objects but keeps their getters linked, so city changes sync back

items.explanation: { ...original } copies only the outer object, so writing draft.address.city changed the original's address. structuredClone copies nested data as well.

items.prompt: `counter` from `makeCounter()` has already been called twice. A new `other = makeCounter()` is created and `console.log(other(), counter())` runs. What prints, and why?

choices.text: `3 4`: both closures read the one `count` declared in makeCounter, so `other` continues it
`1 3`: each makeCounter call creates its own private `count`, so `other` starts fresh
`undefined 3`: `count` only lives while makeCounter runs, so a new closure cannot read it
`1 1`: calling makeCounter again resets the `count` that every earlier closure reads

choices: `3 4`: both closures read the one `count` declared in makeCounter, so `other` continues it
`1 3`: each makeCounter call creates its own private `count`, so `other` starts fresh
`undefined 3`: `count` only lives while makeCounter runs, so a new closure cannot read it
`1 1`: calling makeCounter again resets the `count` that every earlier closure reads

items.explanation: Two closures, two private variables: nothing outside can read or reset count, and each factory call allocates its own, so `other` starts over while `counter` continues from 2.

items.prompt: A cart shows 105 items after "10" from a form plus 5 extra. A teammate proposes wrapping the final result: `Number(quantityInput + extraItems)`. Why is that the wrong fix?

choices.text: It works for 10 + 5 but breaks decimals, because Number() rounds strings to integers
It works, but Number() is slower than parseInt, so parseInt should wrap the result
`+` had already joined the strings into "105"; converting afterwards just gives 105
Number() returns NaN for any concatenated string, so the cart would show NaN

choices: It works for 10 + 5 but breaks decimals, because Number() rounds strings to integers
It works, but Number() is slower than parseInt, so parseInt should wrap the result
`+` had already joined the strings into "105"; converting afterwards just gives 105
Number() returns NaN for any concatenated string, so the cart would show NaN

items.explanation: The damage happened when + concatenated; converting afterwards cannot undo it, so the input must be converted before the arithmetic. Fix the cause, not the symptom: convert at the boundary where the string enters your code and check Number.isNaN.
